To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exposure to high ambient temperature during the first 3 d of life has a significant impact on growth and function of the chick intestinal tract.
thermal conditioning of chicks at an early age alters the expression and activity of brush-border enzymes in a manner that is consistent with the observed changes in feed intake and growth rate.

thermal conditioning at 3 d posthatching causes an immediate effect characterized mainly by lowered triiodothryonine (T3), reduced feed intake, depressed enterocyte proliferation, depressed brush-border membrane (BMM) enzyme activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of thermal stress and thermal conditioning on the growth and development of poultry.
how the environment affects the development of the gastrointestinal tract, and we have demonstrated that the thermal conditioning of the chick alters intestinal structure and function.
the effects of thermal conditioning on the development and functionality of the small intestine of the chicken.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
early thermal conditioning influences intestinal growth and function by modulating T3 concentration, which is associated with changes in feed intake and growth rate.
thermal conditioning affects growth and function of the chick small intestine.
the effects of thermal conditioning on the intestine are mediated by changes in feed intake, which, in turn, are mediated by changes of plasma T3 concentrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thermal conditioning of young chicks is associated with a series of changes in the intestinal structure and function that are related to the level of feed intake.
the effects of thermal conditioning on the intestine are mediated by the effects of thermal treatment on feed intake.
thermal conditioning at 3 d posthatch caused a reduction in feed intake and T3 level, which resulted in a depressed intestinal tract growth and function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
early exposure to heat causes a series of changes in the intestinal epithelium that can be detected at the level of the enterocyte and the BBM.
early thermal conditioning affects the growth and functionality of the intestinal epithelium.
the intestinal tract is a sensitive indicator of environmental stress.
